text: Since he would neither copy nor leave, I gave him six days notice and, when the time was up, handed him thirty two dollars, twenty more than his due, telling him that he must go. <break time="0.8s" /> Proud of my masterly management in assuming his departure, I returned the next morning, only to hear, from behind the screen, the same mild voice reply, I would prefer not to quit you. <break time="0.8s" /> Seized for a moment by a dangerous anger, I recalled how a hasty man in a lonely office had once lost his temper and committed a dreadful deed, and I calmed myself with the thought of charity. <break time="0.8s" /> After reading Edwards on the Will and Priestley on Necessity, I came to believe that Bartleby had been billeted upon me for some mysterious purpose of an all wise Providence. <break time="0.8s" /> But my professional friends, visiting the office, began to whisper about the strange creature I kept there, and a rumor spread that he might outlive me and claim possession of my office by right of his perpetual occupancy. <break time="0.8s" /> Since he would not leave me, I resolved to leave him, and so I moved my offices to another building, saying to him at parting, Good bye, Bartleby, and God some way bless you. <break time="0.8s" /> Soon the new tenant and the landlord came to me in despair, for Bartleby, refusing to depart, now sat upon the banister of the stairs by day and slept in the entry by night. <break time="0.8s" /> I offered him one occupation after another, a clerkship in a store, a bartenders post, a trip to Europe as a companion, and finally my own home, yet he would prefer not to make any change at all.
